messages.author: 573434c2179394c8
messages.subject: drop unused traps?
parts:
Hi Everyone,

I read a recent paper where the authors dropped unused traps from the CR/SCR analysis. Specifically, they dropped rub trees that never yielded a hair sample. What would the advantage/disadvantage of this approach be, as opposed to including all traps? I assume this would inflate the detection probabilities but am not clear on the logic behind dropping sampled traps.

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: drop unused traps?
parts:
Hi Annie

The models assume that a site may be 'never used', and that has always been a problem with 'found' sites like rub trees, that always have a history (also, carnivore latrines etc.). My intuition is that it will have little effect on the density estimates if the study uses only that one type of site, because the detection parameter estimates will adjust. (Combining site types would be more risky). It would be fairly easy to check by simulation - for each replicate dataset just drop the sites with no detections from both the capture and traps parts of the CH object.

Conceptually, one could also fit a 'site-truncated' model in which only used sites appeared, but for that (by intuition, again) you would need to specify the general distribution of potential sites (e.g. uniform across a region). Not impossible, but there would need to be
some motivation (e.g. failure of my earlier intuition).

I'd be interested if others have thought about this.
Murray

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: drop unused traps?
parts:
Taking this a bit further...

Some initial simulations (attached file) show that dropping unvisited* detectors causes definite bias in standard SECR estimates of density. As we both intuited, there is a large bias in the estimate of lambda0, but it goes beyond that. There is definitely a need to tread carefully here (and it is just one of my doubts about rub-tree estimates). The SECR model does not strictly apply even to the more conservative approach of including (recently) unvisited rub trees. Someone should think more deeply about this!

Murray

*We were using the term 'unused' but I have switched to 'unvisited' to avoid conflict with the 'usage' attribute of detectors (which means something else).

messages.author: daaeb91800c54fd1
messages.subject: Re: drop unused traps?
parts:
Hi Annie,

Sorry I missed your email earlier about our decision to drop rub trees with no detections in our open population SCR analysis of grizzly bears. I was on the road.

I decided to remove those rub trees from the analysis because many of those sites were set up by volunteers and staff new to our area. Many of the trees to my eye were not rub trees. Moreover, after three years of data collection they failed to collect a single hair sample. Including these sites in the analysis would in my opinion would cause the model to underestimate detection rates.

Another approach to deal with varying quality of rub trees would be to include a random effect for rub tree. I tried this on some preliminary models and it worked well.

Jesse
